notes.heading: Bonding continuum and the bonding triangle
points: Real bonding is a continuum between ionic, covalent and metallic models, not three separate boxes.
A bonding triangle shows this, with ionic, covalent and metallic at the three corners; the data booklet provides it.
It merges the ionic–covalent continuum (electronegativity difference) with the metallic–covalent continuum (mean electronegativity).
Many materials don't behave typically for their bonding type; mixed bonding explains property variation within a category.

notes.heading: Locating a compound in the triangle
points: Position depends on the relative contributions of ionic, covalent and metallic bonding to the overall bond.
Electronegativity difference Δχ = larger minus smaller value: the ionic–covalent parameter. Higher Δχ means more ionic.
Mean electronegativity χ = (sum of the two values) ÷ 2: the metallic–covalent parameter. Low χ means more metallic.
Electronegativity values come from the data booklet. Only binary compounds are considered; no percentage ionic character calculations.
Same atoms give the same position whatever the bond order or formula, e.g. NO and NO2 share one point.
Examples: CF4 (Δχ 1.4, χ 3.3) polar covalent; Si (Δχ 0, χ 1.9) between metallic and covalent; BaI2 ionic.

notes.heading: Properties of mixed-bonding substances
points: Silicon, between metallic and covalent, is a lustrous, brittle, network-structured semiconductor whose conductivity rises with heat, light or impurities.
Partial covalent character makes experimental lattice enthalpy exceed the purely ionic theoretical value, as in AgCl compared with NaCl.
AlCl3 sits on the ionic/polar covalent boundary: low melting point, forms Al2Cl6 dimers, and dissolves in non-polar solvents.
So the triangle cannot always predict properties, especially for mixed bonding.
Silver halides (more covalent) have melting points depending on London forces; potassium halides (ionic) fall as anion size grows.

notes.heading: Alloys and their enhanced properties
points: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals; the composition ratio can vary.
Alloys keep the delocalized electron sea, so they still conduct and are lustrous.
Atoms of different size disrupt the regular lattice, so layers slide less easily: alloys are harder and stronger than pure metals.
Examples: steel (iron and carbon), bronze (copper and tin), brass (copper and zinc), stainless steel (iron with at least 11% chromium, protective oxide layer).

notes.heading: Polymers: monomers and repeating units
points: Polymers are macromolecules made of many monomers joined end to end by covalent bonds; the process is polymerization.
Draw a repeating unit in brackets with bonds crossing the brackets and subscript n after it.
Natural polymers: starch, cellulose, proteins, DNA, silk. Synthetic: polyethene, nylon, PET, Kevlar.
Polymers are strong with low conductivity, and relatively high melting points because of many intermolecular forces and entangled chains.
Plastics resist biodegradation because they are inert and lack reactive groups; crosslinking limits microbial access.

notes.heading: Addition polymerization of alkenes
points: Monomers contain a C=C double bond; one bond opens and each carbon bonds to a neighbouring monomer.
n CH2=CH2 gives poly(ethene), a chain of n repeating units; no other product forms.
Any monomer with a C=C bond can do this, e.g. chloroethene gives PVC and propene gives polypropene.
PVC is stronger than polyethene because polar C–Cl bonds add dipole–dipole forces to London forces.
To find a monomer from a polymer, take the repeating unit of two chain carbons and restore the double bond.

notes.heading: Condensation polymers and hydrolysis
points: Monomers with two reactive functional groups react to form linkages, releasing a small molecule such as water or HCl each time.
Dicarboxylic acid plus diol gives a polyester with ester linkages, alternating ABAB; water is released.
Dicarboxylic acid plus diamine gives a polyamide (nylon-6,6) with amide linkages; water is released.
A monomer with two different end groups can polymerize with itself, e.g. 3-hydroxypentanoic acid.
2-Amino acids form polypeptides via amide (peptide) bonds, releasing water.
All biological macromolecules form by condensation and break down by hydrolysis, which adds water to split the linkage.

definitions.definition: A mixture of a metal with other metals or non-metals, which has enhanced properties compared with the pure metal.
definitions.trap: Calling an alloy a compound; its component ratio can vary.

definitions.definition: A macromolecule, a very large molecule, made of many repeating subunits (monomers) joined by covalent bonds.
definitions.trap: Forgetting that polymers are built from repeating monomer units.

definitions.definition: A small molecule that joins end to end with others in polymerization to form a polymer chain.
The group of atoms that appears repeatedly along a polymer chain, used to describe the polymer's structure.
definitions.trap: Drawing it without bonds crossing the brackets or without subscript n.

definitions.definition: Monomers containing a C=C double bond join as the double bond breaks, forming a polymer with no other product.
definitions.trap: Saying a small molecule is released; that is condensation.

definitions.definition: Monomers with reactive functional groups at each end react to form linkages, releasing a small molecule such as water for each link.
definitions.trap: Omitting the small molecule that is lost at each linkage.

definitions.definition: The reverse of condensation: a molecule of water splits the linkage formed by condensation.
definitions.trap: Confusing it with condensation, where water is released rather than added.

definitions.definition: A triangular diagram showing bonding as a continuum between ionic, covalent and metallic, positioned by electronegativity difference and mean electronegativity.
definitions.trap: Treating bond types as separate categories instead of a continuum.

definitions.definition: A material with electrical conductivity between conductors and insulators, which increases when heated, illuminated or in the presence of certain impurities.
The breakdown of materials by microorganisms into small molecules.
definitions.trap: Confusing it with microplastics, which stay chemically unchanged.
